newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Transavia sees profit upturn in 1997/98.
newsitem.headline: Transavia sees profit upturn in 1997/98.

text.p: Dutch charter airline Transavia on Tuesday reported net profits fell by almost two thirds in 1996/97 but said it expected a clear improvement in results over the current year as restructuring was starting to pay off.
Transavia, 80 percent owned by Dutch national carrier KLM, said net profits fell to 4.6 million guilders ($2.4 million) in the financial year ended March 31, down from 17.7 million in 1995/96.

However operating profits held steady at 4.53 million guilders compared to a year-earlier 4.52 million. Net profits in 1995/96 were bumped up by a 13.1 million guilder book profit on the sale of three Boeing 737-200 aircraft.
Transavia chairman Pieter Legro said spiralling fuel costs, a stronger dollar and cut-throat industry competition had continued to pressure margins over the year.
Operating costs rose to 545 million guilders from 537 million, although this was partially offset by revenues -- up eight million guilders to 560.40 -- and lower financial charges.
"Just like last year, we earned no more than 1.90 guilders per passenger -- that shows how thin our margins are at present," Legro told an earnings presentation.
"Three years ago we were still making around 10 guilders (per passenger)," he added.
But he said profitability was set to improve over the current year as restructuring measures kicked in.
These included the contracting out of ground-handling services -- including passenger check-in -- at Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport to Ogden Aviation effective November 1.
Transavia has set aside 3.8 million guilders for restructuring, a sum offset by book profits on component sales.

"Measures aimed at structurally improving the cost-income ratio will pay off this year," Legro said. "As a result we expect that the result over the 1997/98 financial year will significantly improve."
But despite the expected upturn in earnings, Transavia would not achieve its targeted 15 percent return on equity, he said.
In 1996/97 returns dwindled to just three percent from a year-earlier 13 percent.
But Legro pointed out that last October the airline had still expected to book a loss over the year, smashing a 17-year track record of unbroken profits.

Transavia avoided falling into the red thanks to a good winter season and a number of ad hoc contracts to lease aircraft and crews to other airlines, including British Airways and Ukraine International Airways, he said.
